title: Goldman Sachs Cuts KOSPI Target Again to 7,500 — a 37.5% Reduction in Five Months
text:
Goldman Sachs Cuts KOSPI Target to 7,500 Again… a 37.5% Reduction in Five Months — BigGo Finance Ask AI News Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers More Ask AI News Watchlist Holdings Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Podcasts Influencers Goldman Sachs Cuts KOSPI Target to 7,500 Again… a 37.5% Reduction in Five Months
 Add preferred source Goldman Sachs has lowered its 12-month KOSPI target to 7,500 from 9,000, a 16.7% cut. That marks a 37.5% reduction in five months since it set a 12,000 target in June, with the bank citing greater second-half volatility and a slower pace of earnings forecast upgrades. It kept its "overweight" rating and judged that memory-sector share prices already reflect an overly harsh scenario of a 70% decline in next-year earnings. The 7,500 level corresponds to a forward P/E of 4.9x, and Goldman projects a 50% 12-month total return in dollar terms even at that level. Morgan Stanley offered a contrasting view, suggesting the KOSPI could settle above 10,000 within three to five years. Key Elements 
 Goldman Sachs KOSPI Samsung Electronics SK Hynix Morgan Stanley High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) DRAM Investing.com Korea Discount Goldman Sachs has cut its 12-month KOSPI target to 7,500 from 9,000. That is a 37.5% reduction in the five months since it set a 12,000 target in June. Despite the lower target, the bank kept its "overweight" investment rating unchanged and maintained a 50% 12-month total return forecast in dollar terms.
 According to financial data provider Investing.com on the 19th, Goldman Sachs lowered its 12-month KOSPI target to 7,500 from 9,000, a 16.7% cut, in a report dated the 17th (local time). The adjustment comes about three weeks after it cut the target to 9,000 from 12,000 on the 25th of last month. Having raised the target to 12,000 on June 3 and held it through the second-half correction in AI-related stocks, the bank has now pulled back that level of expectations in two steps.
 The cautious stance of the market was cited as a key reason for the target cut. The bank's judgment is that, despite a strong first-half rally, market participants are reluctant to fully reflect corporate fundamentals in share prices. It assessed that the South Korean stock market passed through a difficult stretch in the second half marked by high volatility and a slower pace of earnings forecast upgrades, and that doubts about the durability of the memory industry cycle weighed on the index's upside.
 Earnings momentum outside the semiconductor concentration also weakened. According to the report, the projected earnings-per-share (EPS) growth rate for companies excluding Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix soared from 28% in January to 84% in August before retreating to 81% in November. The forecast for next year also fell from 20% in July to 15% in October.

 Still, the bank followed with an assessment that the market's pessimism toward memory semiconductors is excessive. South Korean memory-sector share prices currently reflect a scenario in which next year's earnings consensus (the market forecast) is cut by 70%, which the bank called excessive concern given companies' statements that DRAM and high bandwidth memory (HBM) volumes are sold out through 2029. It projected that the memory supply shortage will continue through 2028 and, at the longest, through 2030. However, it expected the EPS growth rates of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix to slow to 5% and 13%, respectively, in 2028 from 64% and 47% next year.
 It also found investment opportunities in sectors outside memory, on the grounds that valuations (the level of corporate value assessment) have fallen to historic lows. It also viewed the macroeconomic environment favorably. It projected that South Korea's economic growth will slow next year from this year but maintain a solid pace that exceeds both the market forecast and the long-term potential growth rate.
 It also maintained its assessment that the unwinding of the "Korea Discount" (the undervaluation of the South Korean stock market) is continuing. Citing next year's regular shareholder meeting season, expanded shareholder returns and continued governance reform as additional upside catalysts, it said the market has yet to fully reflect the effects of governance improvements. On the supply-demand side, it projected that large-scale share buybacks and light investor positioning (equity holdings) will work favorably.
 Even with the lower target, the expected return remains high. The 7,500 level corresponds to a 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) of 4.9x and a price-to-book ratio (PBR) of 1.18x. Goldman Sachs analyzed that even at this level, the index is more than 40% below fair value. Even applying conservative valuation assumptions, it forecasts a 12-month total return of 50% in US dollar terms.
 The gap in views among global investment banks (IBs) appears to be widening instead. Morgan Stanley said in a report on the 11th that the KOSPI could surpass 10,000 and settle there within three to five years, citing an industrial transformation centered on artificial intelligence (AI), defense and energy, along with capital market reforms. While Goldman Sachs is lowering its target to reflect a slowdown in short-term earnings momentum, Morgan Stanley is placing weight on medium- to long-term structural transformation.
 Some assessments suggest the latest adjustment warrants attention to its direction rather than the target itself. Cutting the target by 37.5% while maintaining an overweight opinion and a 50% total return forecast can be read as lowering the index's upside ceiling, not abandoning a positive view of the South Korean stock market. The judgment that a scenario of downgraded earnings forecasts for the memory sector is already largely reflected in share prices also points to downside rigidity.
 However, the slowing pace of earnings forecast upgrades shows that short-term index momentum may be limited. Given an index structure heavily dependent on earnings from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, in the period when the two companies' 2028 EPS growth rates fall to single digits, the index's upward momentum is likely to shift to non-memory sectors and shareholder return policies. This is read as the backdrop for Goldman Sachs emphasizing both the valuation appeal of non-memory stocks and governance reform.
